t: Maximum Requests Without Violating the Limit — Greedy Rate Limiting per User
o: Independently per user, we keep the most timestamps such that no window of length `window` (inclusive interval [t, t+window]) contains more than k kept requests. Equivalently, no k+1 kept requests may span ≤ window. Example 2: four requests within span 5 > k=2 forces dropping 2. Users are independent, so sum the per-user maxima. Greedy: process a user's sorted times, always keep the current request, and drop the earliest kept request whenever keeping it would violate the limit — an exchange argument shows this is optimal.
k: Users are independent: solve each user separately and add results.
Violation ⇔ some k+1 kept requests lie within a span of `window`; check only the (k+1) most recent kept requests against the new timestamp.
Greedy 'keep current, evict oldest on violation' maximizes the kept count.

a.i: Per user, sort timestamps; maintain a queue of kept times. After appending t, if the queue has more than k elements and the oldest of the newest k+1 is within `window` of t, evict from the front until legal.
s: Bucket timestamps by user; sort each list.
Maintain deque of kept times; append t.
While len(deque) > k and t - deque[len-k-1] <= window, popleft.
a.t: O(R log R) — sorting dominates; each request enters/leaves the queue once (queue indexing is O(k) worst case, still small)

w: One clean greedy per user is the intended solution; a plain list with pop(0) works but is slower. Pitfalls: the interval is inclusive, so 'within window' means difference ≤ window (Example 3); the eviction condition must compare the (k+1)-th newest kept request, not the oldest overall. Follow-up: what if requests arrive online (streaming) — the same greedy works since it never revisits decisions.
